rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.4, own field sampling of salt crusts (EC, thickness, moisture) at nine shelterbelt sites and the research station, 2012-2013. Q2: Section 3.1/Figure 3 and Section 3.3/Figure 5 report, as own results, salt accumulation at the surface during a 10-day drip cycle and crust EC lowest near the emitter, rising to a maximum at ~40 cm and declining outside the wetting front; Section 3.2/Figure 4 reports crust EC rising logarithmically and thickness linearly with drip-water salinity. Q4: Figure 3A measured soil-water content at 0-30 cm in the irrigated area alongside EC through the drying cycle, showing moisture depletion and salt accumulation occurring together, i.e. the evaporation-driven soil-water pathway for crust formation. Q6: Section 3.2/Figure 4 reports crust EC and thickness across nine sites spanning the 436 km drip-irrigated shelterbelt (an irrigation scheme), not a single plot. Q7: Section 3.1 states from own observations that a crust formed only once surface EC reached 1.03 dS/m and moisture fell to 0.6%, and Section 3.2 that higher-salinity water under the same irrigation amount and cycle is what delivers more salt to the surface. Q8: Section 2.1 states the station and the whole shelterbelt were assumed to share one climate because meteorological data exist only at the station; Section 4.3 notes ion composition of water and soil physico-chemical properties were not accounted for; Section 4.1 notes the 7- and 10-year EC-thickness regressions are not robust. Q9: Figures 4, 6 and 7 show error bars of 1 standard deviation for crust EC and thickness; Table 1 gives means <U+00B1> SD.
rows.notes: Study is cited for the second part of the passage (crusts reflecting salt accumulation and redistribution around emitters); the evaporation-inhibition percentages belong to ref [54], not this study. Triangulation is absent: all results come from one sampling-plus-laboratory EC method. Q6 'yes' is given with some doubt: results are from 5 emitters per site aggregated along the scheme rather than a scheme-level mass balance. Representativeness is a single aeolian sand soil and a single assumed climate.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.2.3, own sampling of 40 crust samples in eight radial directions around five emitters on flat sand and five on 15-25 degree south-facing dune slopes, June 2013. Q2: Section 3.3/Figure 5 reports that on dune slopes the highest crust EC appeared at 20-30 cm upslope of the emitter but at 40-50 cm downslope, with upslope EC higher than downslope, and on flat land EC was higher to the east, south and west than to the north.
rows.notes: The passage closely matches Section 3.3. Q4 'no': the mechanisms offered (gravity-driven downslope wetting-front advance, plant shade reducing evaporation on the north side) are asserted in Section 4.2, not measured for the slope sites; soil water was measured only in the flat irrigated area in the cycle study. Q5 'no': only two topography types on one sandy soil in one climate. Q6 'no': the spatial pattern is reported at the emitter (0-50 cm) scale near the research station. Q7 'no': emitter-placement advice (north side, upslope) is a recommendation, and slope angle is a factor the pattern varied with, not a stated requirement. Q8 'no': no limitation is stated specifically for the spatial-distribution result (the single-climate assumption concerns the salinity comparison). Q9 'no': Figure 5 shows spatially averaged contour maps with no dispersion measure for the directional EC values.

notes: Full text appears complete though OCR-duplicated in places. Primary observational field study of soil salt crusts under saline drip irrigation along the Taklimakan Desert Highway Shelterbelt; all results rely on one method (field sampling with vernier-caliper thickness and 1:5 extract EC).
